Blind Spot Navigation in Large Language Model Reasoning
with Thought Space Explorer
Jinghan Zhang1, Fengran Mo2, Tharindu Cyril Weerasooriya3,
Xinyue Ye4,Dongjie Wang 5,Yanjie Fu 6,Kunpeng Liu 1*
1Clemson University, 2Université de Montréal, 3Center for Advanced AI, Accenture,
4The University of Alabama, 5University of Kansas, 6Arizona State University
{jinghaz,kunpenl}@clemson.edu
Abstract
Large language models have shown strong rea-
soning capabilities through chain-structured
methods such as Chain-of-Thought. Recent
studies optimize thought structures by gener-
ating parallel or tree-like structures, switching
long and short reasoning modes, or aligning
reasoning steps with task performance. How-
ever, these approaches mainly rely on previ-
ously generated logical directions of the chains,
which ignore the unexplored regions of the so-
lution space. Such a phenomenon is denoted
asblind spots, which limit the diversity and
effectiveness of the reasoning process. To this
end, we propose the “Thought Space Explorer”
(TSE), a framework for navigating and expand-
ing thought structures to overcome blind spots
in LLM reasoning. Our TSE first identifies key
nodes with high impact, then generates new
nodes by integrating information from multi-
ple chains. Finally, it extends new branches
through connection strategies. We conduct a
series of experiments on math and QA bench-
marks. Compared to existing baseline methods,
TSE improves the accuracy of both the final
answer and intermediate reasoning steps, while
maintaining a better effectiveness-efficiency
trade-off for practical deployment.
1 Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
have shown great potential in solving complex
tasks with reasoning capabilities (Huang and
Chang, 2022; Patterson et al., 2022; Achiam et al.,
2023; Mao et al., 2023; Dutta et al., 2025) by
guiding the LLMs to logically solve the complex
task step-by-step. A common practice is to design

{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Aintrinsic+motivation+mechanisms+for+autonomous+goal+discovery&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: Where do goals come from? A Generic Approach to Autonomous Goal-System Development
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1410.5557v1
published: 2014-10-21T07:24:03Z
summary: Goals express agents' intentions and allow them to organize their behavior based on low-dimensional abstractions of high-dimensional world states. How can agents develop such goals autonomously? This paper proposes a detailed conceptual and computational account to this longstanding problem. We argue to consider goals as high-level abstractions of lower-level intention mechanisms such as rewards and values, and point out that goals need to be considered alongside with a detection of the own actions' effects. We propose Latent Goal Analysis as a computational learning formulation thereof, and show constructively that any reward or value function can by explained by goals and such self-detection as latent mechanisms. We first show that learned goals provide a highly effective dimensionality reduction in a practical reinforcement learning problem. Then, we investigate a developmental scenario in which entirely task-unspecific rewards induced by visual saliency lead to self and goal representations that constitute goal-directed reaching.

title: Control Strategies for Autonomous Vehicles
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2011.08729v3
published: 2020-11-17T16:04:39Z
summary: This chapter focuses on the self-driving technology from a control perspective and investigates the control strategies used in autonomous vehicles and advanced driver-assistance systems from both theoretical and practical viewpoints. First, we introduce the self-driving technology as a whole, including perception, planning and control techniques required for accomplishing the challenging task of autonomous driving. We then dwell upon each of these operations to explain their role in the autonomous system architecture, with a prime focus on control strategies. The core portion of this chapter commences with detailed mathematical modeling of autonomous vehicles followed by a comprehensive discussion on control strategies. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=Can+falsification+of+core+reward-scalarization+assumptions+be+automated+in+reinforcement+learning+architectures%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6836287\", \"title\": [\"Research on Trajectory Planning for Automated Vehicles Based on Reinforcement Learning in Sparse Reward Environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Trajectory planning for automated vehicles in complex and dynamic environments is the core issue of automated driving systems. Dynamic obstacles and nonlinear road conditions in complicated traffic scenarios pose severe challenges to the stability and adaptability of planning algorithms. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning fails to converge efficiently under sparse reward conditions, resulting in low learning efficiency and unstable trajectories. To solve the above problems, this paper proposes a reinforcement learning-based trajectory planning model for automated vehicles, namely the Intrinsic Curiosity Module–Progress Hindsight Experience Replay (ICM-PHER). This model introduces an intrinsic reward mechanism driven by prediction error to facilitate effective exploration, thereby alleviating training inefficiency caused by sparse rewards. Combined with curriculum learning, a dynamic target point guidance strategy is designed to enable vehicles to learn gradually from simple tasks to complex ones. Furthermore, an improved Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) mechanism integrated with a dynamic filtering sampler is adopted to remove low-quality experiences and improve the utilization efficiency of valid samples. A multi-scenario automated driving simulation platform is established to verify the performance of the proposed model. Experimental results show that compared with baseline methods, the ICM-PHER model delivers up to 300% higher average reward in sparse reward and complex scenarios, reduces training collisions by about 60%, and increases key indicators including speed and trajectory length by 23%–230%. The proposed method greatly boosts exploration efficiency and trajectory planning performance, and effectively improves the trajectory planning efficiency and complex environment adaptability of automated vehicles in sparse reward settings.</jats:p>\", …

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=metrics+for+evaluating+autonomous+scientific+discovery+agents+and+research+agendas&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"title\": [\"A Brief History of AI for Scientific Discovery: Open Research, Metrics, and Autonomous Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The history of artificial intelligence for scientific discovery is not a two year story about chatbots learning to write papers. It is a sixty year story about science repeatedly handing its bottlenecks to machines—first inference, then search, then measurement, then the full workflow—only to discover that each delegation solves one problem and exposes a harder one underneath. This paper traces that history from DENDRAL (1965) through the construction of open scholarly infrastructure (arXiv, Google Scholar, ORCID), the oracle breakthroughs of AlphaFold, and the current era of LLM driven autonomous research agents. Three interlocking threads are followed including AI as research instrument, AI for research infrastructure, and the reshaping of scholarly profiles and incentives by machine readable metrics. The central tension throughout is between automation and augmentation between building systems that replace human researchers and tools that amplify human creativity and judgement. The paper presents that the most consequential development is not any single tool but the emergence of an interconnected ecosystem where AI agents, preprint platforms, open source codebases, and citation infrastructure form a feedback loop that is fundamentally restructuring who can do science, how fast discoveries propagate, and what counts as a valid scientific contribution.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 3, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/gnwd5518\", \"title\": [\"Better Metrics for Evaluating Explainable Artificial Intelligence\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper presents objective metrics for how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can be quantified.
